briefing.title: What Devoteam is
briefing.text: An EMEA-focused technology consultancy positioning itself as AI-driven tech consulting. The About page markets 11,000 people across 25+ countries; a July 2026 sustainability page gives an exact count of 10,197 in 25 countries.

briefing.title: Why Portugal matters
briefing.text: Devoteam says Portugal passed €100M in revenue with 1,400+ specialists and is central to its 2026 push from AI experimentation to production and measurable ROI.

briefing.title: What the role does
briefing.text: Build end-to-end ML pipelines, turn prototypes into production-grade Python, deploy on cloud infrastructure, and monitor models, drift, and reliability.

briefing.title: How to position yourself
briefing.text: Lead with forecasting over 1M+ records, hierarchical anomaly-detection research, a tested Dockerized FastAPI AI system, and ownership of a live client service.

briefing.title: Evidence discipline
briefing.text: Separate tools you have operated from concepts you can explain. Lead with tested Python services, Docker, CI, reproducible workflows, and live production ownership.

briefing.title: Best opening question
briefing.text: I found both the AI/Machine Learning Engineer and MLOps vacancies under Distributed Cloud. Which description is closest to this project?

items.title: Strategy
items.text: Devoteam says 2025 was the year of AI experimentation and 2026 is the year of AI value: move pilots into production with real ROI.

items.title: Leadership
items.text: A 4 September 2026 announcement names Nuno Oliveira Santos as General Director for Portugal and group Vice President for the global Microsoft pillar.

items.title: Data & AI practice
items.text: The 2024 Singularity integration announcement reported 100+ Data & AI specialists in Portugal and about 1,000 across EMEA.

items.title: Delivery footprint
items.text: Official listings include Lisbon, Porto, and Aveiro; leadership describes Portugal as a competence and international delivery center.

items.title: 2024 group snapshot
items.text: The 2024 CSR report states €1.158B revenue, €119M operating margin, and 10,171 employees at 31 December 2024.

items.title: Latest CSR headcount
items.text: Devoteam's July 2026 sustainability page states 10,197 employees in 25 countries, while its marketing block on the same page still rounds to 11,000 specialists.

items.title: Amplify 2028
items.text: The group strategy targets €2B revenue in 2028, 50% of revenue from AI projects, and generative-AI training for all employees.

items.title: Strategy copy also conflicts
items.text: English and French Amplify releases published on the same day used different 2024 AI-share targets and project counts. Treat the 2028 direction as firmer than the interim figures.

items.title: Likely meaning
items.text: In this vacancy, Distributed Cloud appears to be the business unit connecting cloud engineering, managed services, and ML delivery rather than a narrow product name.

items.title: Operational scope
items.text: Public material covers public and hybrid cloud, cost, compliance, security, cloud data, and managed AI across AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure.

items.title: Not the Google product by default
items.text: Devoteam separately holds Google Distributed Cloud product expertise. Public evidence does not establish that this Portugal vacancy is a Google Distributed Cloud role.

items.title: Unknown project context
items.text: The client, reporting line, geography, primary cloud, team composition, and on-call model are not public.

items.title: Corporate figures differ by page
items.text: The About page rounds to 11,000 people; CSR sources state 10,171 at year-end 2024 and 10,197 in July 2026; job templates still say 10,000+. Name the source and date when precision matters.

items.title: Partner counts vary
items.text: The Databricks page uses different certification totals in different passages. Say Devoteam has a substantial certified practice rather than quoting one exact count.

stories.title: Demand forecasting over 1M+ records
stories.summary: Built a demand-forecasting pipeline over more than one million sales records for inventory-oriented planning.

star.situation: High-volume transactional data with time-dependent demand.
star.task: Turn raw sales records into a repeatable forecasting workflow.
star.action: Discuss validation, time-aware splits, lag and rolling features, baselines, metrics, and reproducible processing.
star.result: An end-to-end forecasting pipeline over 1M+ records.
star.reflection: For production: data tests, experiment tracking, registry, drift monitoring, scheduled retraining, and fallback forecasts.

stories.boundary: Documented scope: a forecasting pipeline over 1M+ records for inventory-oriented planning.

stories.title: Hierarchical time-series anomaly detection
stories.summary: Thesis research on anomaly detection in hierarchical and grouped multidimensional time series.

star.situation: Anomalies may appear at leaf, aggregate, or cross-series levels while labels are scarce.
star.task: Define and evaluate a hierarchy-aware approach.
star.action: Define anomaly taxonomy, preserve time order, avoid leakage, separate model score from alert policy, and plan feedback.
star.result: A structured research program connecting time-series methods to operational monitoring.
star.reflection: Production evaluation should include alert utility, label delay, root-cause workflow, and human feedback.

stories.boundary: Documented scope: coursework complete; thesis research remains in progress.

stories.title: Tested, Dockerized Python AI service
stories.summary: Built a legal retrieval-augmented generation system spanning five Portuguese tribunals and EU legislation.

star.situation: Legal retrieval needs traceable, relevant results across heterogeneous sources.
star.task: Build a maintainable Python retrieval and API pipeline.
star.action: Separate ingestion, retrieval, reranking, generation, and API concerns; validate schemas; test components; package with Docker.
star.result: A working tested service with hybrid retrieval and clear boundaries.
star.reflection: For production: evaluation data, traces, SLOs, access controls, artifact versions, and staged rollout.

stories.boundary: Documented scope: a tested Dockerized FastAPI service with hybrid retrieval across named legal sources.

stories.title: Live SaaS ownership
stories.summary: Delivered and maintains a live fitness-coaching SaaS for a paying client using managed cloud services.
evidence: Replaced a prior setup costing about €150/month

star.situation: A client needed a maintainable service without the previous server overhead.
star.task: Deliver the product and own ongoing operation.
star.action: Choose managed components, deploy, handle failures, maintain the service, and communicate trade-offs.
star.result: A live service replacing a setup costing approximately €150 per month.
star.reflection: The work built practical instincts about reliability, cost, releases, and ownership that transfer to ML services.

stories.boundary: Documented scope: a live client service and the approximately €150 monthly cost of the previous setup.

technical.title: ML lifecycle
technical.model: A model is production-ready only when data, code, artifact, deployment, monitoring, and recovery are controlled together.
framework: Start with the decision and success metric.
Name failure modes and quality gates.
Finish with ownership, observability, and rollback.
questions: Design a pipeline from notebook to production.
What does production-ready mean?
How would you retrain safely?

cards.a: CI validates code, tests, schemas, and builds. CD promotes an approved artifact. CT retrains and evaluates on a trigger; promotion still needs quality gates.

cards.q: What belongs in a model registry?
cards.a: Immutable artifacts and lineage: code, data, environment, metrics, signatures, owner, approval, and deployment history.
Model, preprocessing, and feature definitions may need to roll back together under one compatible contract.

technical.title: Monitoring and drift
technical.model: Monitor system, data, model, and business health separately; distribution shift is not automatically model failure.
framework: Choose investigation, retraining, recalibration, or rollback.
questions: How do you detect drift?
What if labels arrive late?
What triggers retraining?

cards.a: Data drift changes P(X); concept drift changes P(Y|X). Labels are usually needed to confirm the latter.
No. Confirm impact and diagnose expected change, transient shift, data bug, or true relationship change.

cards.q: Ground truth is delayed. Now what?
cards.a: Use proxy and input/prediction signals early, then backfill true quality metrics when labels arrive.

technical.title: Forecasting
technical.model: The core risks are leakage, weak baselines, the wrong decision metric, and unreliable refresh.
revision: MAE, RMSE, WAPE, MASE, and sMAPE
Why MAPE is unstable near zero
framework: Define grain, horizon, cadence, and decision.
Explain metrics, refresh, monitoring, and fallback.
questions: How would you validate demand forecasts?
Which metric would you choose?
How would you handle new products?

cards.a: It leaks future information. Use time-ordered or rolling-origin splits that match deployment.
It reveals whether complexity adds value beyond repeatable seasonality.

cards.q: How do you choose a metric?
cards.a: Match the decision cost and data shape, report by slices, and avoid unstable percentage errors near zero.

technical.title: Anomaly detection
technical.model: A detector is an alerting system: threshold, context, triage capacity, feedback, and cost of misses all matter.
framework: Evaluate false-positive burden and close the feedback loop.
questions: How do you evaluate without labels?
How do you reduce false positives?
What changes with hierarchy?

cards.a: Rare anomalies make always-normal predictions look accurate. Use precision/recall, PR-AUC, alert burden, and delay.
Costs of misses and false alerts, analyst capacity, calibration, and desired detection delay.
A value normal globally but abnormal for its time, season, segment, or hierarchy level.

technical.title: Feature stores
technical.model: A feature store governs reusable, point-in-time-correct features across training and inference; it is not just a shared table.
framework: Start from reuse and latency needs.
Acknowledge when one batch model does not need it.
questions: What problem does it solve?
How do you prevent skew?
When would you not build one?

cards.a: Training rows use only feature values available at that historical prediction timestamp.
Offline supports historical bulk training retrieval; online supports low-latency current inference features.
One batch model with simple owned features, little reuse, and no low-latency serving need.

technical.title: Docker, Kubernetes, and cloud
technical.model: Package a deterministic workload, expose safe operating signals, and choose managed components from workload and SLO needs.
framework: Map to a cloud only after requirements.
questions: How would you deploy on Kubernetes?
Readiness versus liveness?
How would you choose a cloud ML service?

cards.a: Readiness controls traffic eligibility; liveness decides whether a stuck workload should restart.
Requests guide scheduling; limits bound use. Bad values cause throttling, OOM kills, or waste.
When decisions tolerate latency and predictions can be precomputed; it is usually simpler and cheaper.

technical.title: MLflow, Kubeflow, Airflow, and DVC
technical.model: These tools occupy different lifecycle layers; discuss the problem each solves instead of treating them as substitutes.
revision: MLflow: experiments, artifacts, registry, and champion/challenger aliases
framework: Connect it to review and deployment gates.
questions: What would you track in MLflow?
Kubeflow versus Airflow?
How would you version data?

cards.a: MLflow tracks experiments, artifacts, and model metadata; Airflow schedules and coordinates arbitrary DAG tasks.
Kubernetes is general orchestration; Kubeflow adds ML-oriented workflow components and conventions.

cards.q: What does DVC add to Git?
cards.a: It versions references and pipelines for large artifacts stored outside Git in remote storage.

technical.title: Serving, scale, and rollout
technical.model: Choose the freshness the decision needs, then use the least complex serving architecture that meets its latency, reliability, and cost target.
revision: Batch, online, and streaming decision latency
SLOs for freshness, p95 latency, and availability
Replica scaling, queues, batching, and caching
Shadow, canary, blue/green, and A/B rollout
framework: State decision latency and write pattern.
Close with failure handling, rollback, and cost.
questions: When would you refuse real-time serving?
How would you scale a model API?
How do shadow and canary deployments differ?

cards.a: The challenger scores live traffic while users still receive the champion result, enabling comparison without changing decisions.
It is usually cheaper, simpler to backfill, and easier to operate when the business can tolerate delayed predictions.

cards.q: Two ways to increase throughput without more replicas?
cards.a: Batch compatible requests and cache safe repeated results; profiling may also justify model optimization.

technical.title: Cloud architecture
technical.model: Draw storage, compute, orchestration, registry, serving, monitoring, identity, and cost first; map vendor services second.
revision: AWS: S3, SageMaker, ECR/EKS, CloudWatch, IAM
GCP: GCS, BigQuery, Vertex AI, GKE/Cloud Run, Cloud Monitoring
Azure: ADLS, Synapse, Data Factory, Azure ML, AKS, Azure Monitor
framework: Use data location and workload requirements to choose services.
Ask which partner ecosystem the client already runs.
questions: How would this differ across AWS, GCP, and Azure?
Managed ML platform or Kubernetes?
How do you control training and inference cost?

cards.a: Data store, transform/train, registry, serve, monitor, identity/network, and cost controls.
Keeping training and features near the client's governed data platform reduces transfer, latency, cost, and security complexity.

cards.q: When prefer a managed ML platform?
cards.a: When its lifecycle services meet requirements and the team benefits more from reduced operations than from custom platform control.

technical.title: Testing ML systems
technical.model: Test deterministic contracts and useful behavioral invariants now; judge model quality through a frozen evaluation and promotion contract.
revision: Unit tests for transformations and edge cases
Schema, range, freshness, and leakage tests
Prediction shape, bounds, and invariant checks
API contract, auth, timeout, and load tests
framework: Split code, data, model, pipeline, and serving tests.
Separate CI failures from promotion failures.
State what only production or delayed labels can prove.
questions: How do you unit-test ML?
What fails the build versus model promotion?
How do you test when labels arrive late?

cards.a: A small versioned fixture where predictions or metrics must remain within a justified tolerance after a change.

cards.q: A test that needs no fresh labels?
cards.a: Schema, missingness, freshness, prediction-range, or API-contract checks.

cards.q: Why avoid exact accuracy assertions in CI?
cards.a: CI should protect deterministic contracts; model promotion should evaluate quality against a frozen dataset with explicit tolerances.

interviewQuestions.question: Tell me about yourself.
interviewQuestions.why: Tests relevance, communication, timeline, and motivation.
guide: Lead with ML/AI engineering in Portugal.
Name forecasting, anomaly detection, and production Python.
Use the 1M+ pipeline, research, tested service, and live SaaS.
Close with moving models into reliable cloud systems.
interviewQuestions.sample: I am a machine-learning and AI engineer based in Portugal, with hands-on work across forecasting, anomaly detection, and Python AI services. I built a forecasting pipeline over more than one million records, I am researching hierarchical time-series anomaly detection, and I built a tested, Dockerized FastAPI retrieval system. I also maintain a live SaaS for a paying client, which has given me practical ownership of deployment, reliability, and cost trade-offs. I now want to deepen that production ML path.
interviewQuestions.watch: Keep it under 90 seconds; do not list every technology.

interviewQuestions.question: Why Devoteam?
interviewQuestions.why: Tests whether your interest is specific and informed.
interviewQuestions.sample: Devoteam's focus on moving AI from experiments into production matches the direction I want to deepen. The Data & AI practice in Portugal and the Salvador Caetano forecasting case show the combination of ML, cloud engineering, and measurable client value that attracts me.
interviewQuestions.watch: Do not answer only with the Tech for People slogan.

interviewQuestions.question: What kind of role are you looking for?
interviewQuestions.why: Calibrates the model-development and platform split.
guide: Ownership from data and evaluation to service and monitoring.
interviewQuestions.sample: A hands-on ML engineering role where I can own meaningful lifecycle parts, from data and evaluation through production Python, deployment, and monitoring, while learning from engineers with deeper platform experience.
interviewQuestions.watch: Stay flexible enough for more than one project.

interviewQuestions.question: How strong are you in Kubernetes, MLflow, or feature stores?
guide: State the exact hands-on depth for each named tool.
Name Docker, tests, CI, APIs, data pipelines, and production ownership.
Give a concrete learning and implementation path.
interviewQuestions.sample: I separate direct hands-on depth from conceptual knowledge. My delivery evidence includes tested Python services, Docker, CI, reproducible workflows, and production ownership. For each platform named in the role, I can state the exact depth and explain how it fits registry, deployment, monitoring, and rollback.
interviewQuestions.watch: Pair learning claims with adjacent implementation evidence.

interviewQuestions.question: How does your experience meet the three-year requirement?
guide: Separate client software and AI delivery, academic research, and projects.
Connect transferable production engineering to the role.
Ask how the team weights adjacent delivery evidence.
interviewQuestions.sample: My background combines independent production software and AI delivery, focused ML projects, and thesis research. I would walk through the exact timeline for each category and connect the transferable production work in tested Python services, cloud delivery, and ongoing client ownership to this role.
interviewQuestions.watch: Use a precise timeline and evidence category for every claim.

interviewQuestions.question: Is your master's complete?
interviewQuestions.why: The role lists an advanced degree.
interviewQuestions.sample: The coursework is complete and the thesis is in progress. The research focuses on anomaly detection in hierarchical multidimensional time series.

interviewQuestions.question: Design a pipeline from notebook to production.
interviewQuestions.why: Directly tests the core role mandate.
guide: Track experiments and register immutable artifacts.
Test, package, stage, monitor, retrain, and roll back.
interviewQuestions.sample: I would start with the decision contract and acceptance metric, build point-in-time-correct data and evaluation, track code/data/environment with experiments, register an immutable artifact after quality gates, package batch or API serving, deploy progressively, and monitor system, data, model, and business health with a defined rollback path.
interviewQuestions.watch: Do not make the answer a tool-name list.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you detect and respond to model drift?
interviewQuestions.why: Monitoring and drift are explicit responsibilities.
guide: Separate data, concept, and performance change.
Tie alerts to investigation, retraining, recalibration, or rollback.
interviewQuestions.sample: I would monitor schemas, feature and prediction distributions, system health, and delayed ground-truth metrics by important slices. A drift alert starts diagnosis; it does not automatically trigger retraining. The action depends on confirmed impact and root cause.
interviewQuestions.watch: Drift is not synonymous with performance degradation.

interviewQuestions.question: Tell me about a pipeline or production failure.
interviewQuestions.why: The recruiter explicitly joked about failed pipelines.
guide: Finish with the prevention added afterward.
interviewQuestions.watch: Do not invent an outage; choose a documented project or client-service incident.

facts: Related public vacancies are full-time permanent contracts.
Devoteam is a consultancy, so client allocation can materially shape the work.
The company publicly emphasizes learning, certifications, diversity, and internal mobility.
Portuguese offices are listed in Lisbon, Porto, and Aveiro.
anecdotes: Crowd-sourced reviews contain both positive reports about colleagues, learning, and work-life balance and negative reports about compensation, project allocation, and management consistency.
These reviews are self-selected, may be stale, and may refer to different teams or countries.
verify: Base versus total package and benefits
